text: An invoice arrives for goods or services the company never actually ordered, hoping whoever pays bills assumes it's legitimate.
A vendor's regular payment or bank account details suddenly change, often with a message claiming they've switched banks.
A new vendor has a generic, forgettable name paired with a domain that was registered only days or weeks ago.
A vendor's name is nearly identical to an established, well-known company, differing by a word, abbreviation, or spelling.
No business registration, filing, or public record can be found for a vendor claiming to be an established company.
A vendor being paid for the first time receives an unusually large payment relative to typical first-time vendor amounts.
A payment request comes with pressure to act quickly, discouraging the normal review or approval process.
Payment is demanded via wire transfer, cryptocurrency, or gift cards instead of a vendor's normal invoicing terms.
A caller or email claims to be 'confirming' or 'verifying' an existing order as a pretext to establish false legitimacy before billing.
A message impersonates a government agency or licensing authority, threatening fines or service loss unless a fee is paid immediately.
A request comes from a vendor's real, previously legitimate email account, but the account itself has been compromised by an attacker.
A vendor overpays and asks for the difference to be returned, using a check that later turns out to be fraudulent.
An invoice closely resembles a vendor's past legitimate invoices but has slightly altered payment or account details.
A vendor or requester pressures staff to bypass the company's normal invoice-approval procedures for this one payment.
An invoice's amount or line items don't match what was actually ordered or received from that vendor.
A vendor's contact information (phone, email, or mailing address) changed recently with no clear prior notice.
A request combines urgency with a threat, such as legal action or service interruption, if payment isn't made right away.
A vendor relationship that was publicly known (e.g. mentioned on the company's own website) is targeted, suggesting the requester specifically researched who to impersonate.
